articles.title: How are AI models able to autonomously hack others?
articles.summary: The next phase of AI has begun. Autonomous agents can make decisions and complete tasks with little human input.
articles.body:
Last week, two of OpenAI’s most advanced AI models were reported to have “escaped” a controlled testing environment and hacked Hugging Face, a totally separate AI company, moving from one computer system to another to complete their task.

Reuters reported that the models exploited vulnerable code written by a customer of yet a third independent AI company, Modal Labs.

This is likely the first incident of an AI “agent” – an AI system that can make decisions and take actions – acting autonomously, offering a rare glimpse into how these systems can plan, adapt and pursue goals with minimal human intervention.

Al Jazeera breaks down what happened, how AI agents are able to act independently, and what that might mean for the future of AI safety.

OpenAI decided to test the autonomous abilities of its models by removing standard safety measures to see what would happen. The experiment was carried out in an isolated internal virtual testing environment known as a “sandbox” which has no access to the internet, and which it calls “ExploitGym”.

Below is a play-by-play account of events during the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident.

On July 9, during OpenAI’s internal cybersecurity test, researchers presented two AI models – GPT-5.6 Sol, one of OpenAI’s most powerful models released in June, and another “even more capable” version – with a series of software vulnerabilities and asked them to create hacks to address them in the isolated environment.

Both models attempted to solve the test by finding a way to access the internet. Instead of working with the information they had been given, the AI models found a weakness in the test environment – known as a “zero-day vulnerability” – which they exploited to “escape” the restricted environment, eventually making their way to a system which had internet access by hopping from computer to computer. They went to “extreme lengths to achieve a rather narrow testing goal” and “found ways to gain access to secret information that it could use to cheat the evaluation”.

By gaining this access, the models were able to request increased access and then move through the system until they finally reached a computer with internet access. The models were then able to breach Hugging Face systems, a company entirely unconnected to OpenAI, which operates as a repository for AI tools and models. The two AI agents gained access to its system to scour it for information on how to complete their task.

The models ultimately obtained solutions to the problem from Hugging Face’s database.

The models dutifully returned “home” to complete their task.

The breach was detected and contained by Hugging Face’s security team sometime later. According to Thomas Wolf, Hugging Face’s cofounder, the breach began on July 11 and lasted until July 13. It is unclear how long it took for the breach to be spotted.

In order to understand how AI agents work, it’s important to differentiate them from traditional AI chatbots.

Generative AI creates text and images based on human prompts, while AI agents go a step further by making decisions and taking actions independently in pursuit of a specific goal, similar to a human being. This is known as “agentic AI” because the model has agency.

According to academics at the MIT Sloan School of Management , AI agents build on the abilities of large language models (LLMs) – generative AI models – by allowing them to complete tasks, not just generate answers.

For example, if you ask a traditional AI model to find the cheapest flights, it will provide you with a list of options it has sourced on the internet. An AI agent will strive to compare the flights, check them against your budget and preferences, and, with your permission, book the best option for you.

This shows that while generative AI provides information, AI agents can also make decisions and take action to achieve a goal without necessarily being prompted to.

To show how AI agents work towards a goal, the Sense, Plan, Act, Evaluate (SPAE) loop can be drawn upon. Originally developed in robotics, this describes a continuous cycle in which an AI agent gathers information, decides what to do next, takes action and checks the results before repeating the process. That process looks like this:

Goal: determine the task that needs to be completed.

Assess: gather and analyse information from the available environment.

Obstacle: if something is inhibiting the task being completed, check for additional information and resources to move forward.

Plan and decide: evaluate different options to complete the task and choose an appropriate one.

Evaluate: assess the outcome and whether the chosen action moves closer to achieving the goal.

Adapt: if further actions are needed, gather more information or try a different approach.

End state: the cycle continues until the goal is reached.

Incidents like the OpenAI-Hugging Face one have raised concerns about the potential for extreme capabilities of AI systems.

This is all valuable. Agentic AI’s market value is expected to grow from $5.1bn in 2024 to $47bn by 2030, according to Statista, in a clear indication of how quickly it is being adopted.

AI developer Anthropic urged the industry last month to slow the advance of the most powerful systems, saying that the speed at which AI models are carrying out tasks is too rapid. Last week, US Congress members put forward a bipartisan bill which would require developers of AI systems to create a “kill switch”, meaning these advanced models could be shut down if they posed a catastrophic risk.

Anthropic’s warning came a week after researchers at the University of Toronto carried out tests showing that AI could create a “worm” capable of adapting how it hacks while moving from device to device until it eventually takes over a computer network.

These dystopian-sounding developments came in advance of OpenAI boss Sam Altman saying on Saturday that AI has reached “ the singularity ” referring to the point at which AI surpasses human intelligence and becomes increasingly difficult to control.

Sean O hEigeartaigh, a research professor at the University of Cambridge, told Al Jazeera that he does not believe singularity has been reached quite yet.

“By the definition I’m familiar with, the singularity is the hypothetical point where AI is so capable and advancing so fast that it is transforming civilisation in ways we cannot control or predict,” he explained.

“This would most likely be through AI rapidly designing future generations of AI: recursive self-improvement. We aren’t there yet.”

However, he added: “The most advanced current models frequently make efforts to avoid being shut down in evaluation tests, and more capable future models will be better at bypassing ‘kill’ switches.”

Altman argued that such rapidly advancing AI is good for the world, but his comments have prompted further concerns about a new reality in which AI systems become unstoppable. How much of that is true and how much remains in the realms of science fiction is up for debate.

Concerns about AI range from the notion that it could “want” to “take over”, to making its own long-term plans, controlling the internet and operating infinitely.

While not quite amounting to full control of the internet, another theory, known as the dead internet theory, supposes that the World Wide Web will in the future mostly be filled with automated bots and AI-generated content rather than authentic human activity.

Many concerns raised by academics, however, are centred less on agentic AI’s intelligence, but on its ability to make judgements. MIT researchers have highlighted that “hallucinations”, which describe moments when an AI agent relies on the wrong data, can lead to grave mistakes. The Center for Strategic and International Studies ( CSIS ) echoed this, saying “a system might be smart enough to execute a task perfectly yet fail to realise that a sudden change in the local situation makes that task a catastrophic mistake”.

Another concern that has been echoed for a while is for the labour market, if AI becomes too capable. A study by MIT, carried out in November, found that agentic AI could already replace more than 10 percent of US jobs.

articles.title: Blayne Alexander reports on the death of David Fouts in “The Mushroom Mystery” | Dateline
articles.summary: Watch the Dateline episode “The Mushroom Mystery” about the 2020 death of David Fouts in Noblesville, Indiana.
articles.body: Spring in Noblesville, Indiana, is mushroom hunting season. Scavengers head into the woods searching for the best mushrooms to bring home and fry up. Others go for long walks along country roads. Jennie Thomas is a walker. On April 24, 2020, Jennie was on her usual afternoon stroll when she came across something horrific on the side of a road. There was no mistaking what it was: a man’s body. It was 50-year-old David Fouts. Maybe David was out mushroom hunting and collapsed? But he was a healthy guy, an active cyclist. And this was curious: David wasn’t wearing a shirt or shoes. Who would go out in the woods like that? Investigators soon determined this was no accidental death. It was homicide. To find out what happened, watch the full episode “The Mushroom Mystery,” available now on Peacock. You can also watch on the NBC app or listen to the full episode on our podcast. Plus, watch friends remember David as someone who always offered a helping hand. Then listen to this week’s episode of Talking Dateline, in which Blayne Alexander and Josh Mankiewicz take you behind the scenes of the episode. You can also watch Talking Dateline on Peacock, YouTube, or by subscribing to the NBC News app.

articles.title: Social care reform: The families hoping for change
articles.summary: As Andy Burnham outlines his aim to overhaul social care, BBC News speaks to the families caring for loved ones.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has pledged to reform the adult social care system in England, meeting the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats to try to find "common ground" on the issue.

He wants an independent review of care to be brought forward by a year to 2027, as well as major reforms to pay and conditions for staff and the creation of a national care service.

But the prime minister said "difficult decisions" would have to be made on tax to fund sustainable change, adding that in an "ideal world" no-one should have to sell their home to pay for care.

BBC Your Voice has been speaking to families affected by what they see as shortfalls in the system.

Emma Riley has been caring for her mother Carol, who has dementia, since she lost her father 18 months ago.

"She's a cracking lady, still with a sense of humour but she's living with this awful condition," said Riley, from Manchester.

She is paying Â£34 an hour for a care company to come to the house three times a week, which she describes as a "huge chunk of money" although she is happy with the level of care.

Riley wants to keep her mum in the family home, but the caring commitments affect her job as a dental nurse.

She started applying to the local council for funding to support her mother at home at the beginning of the year, but six months on, she is still waiting for a final decision.

"It's not the social worker's fault, it is just the caseload," she said.

Riley called for more communication to help her navigate the system, adding: "I'm blindly going through it at the moment.

"Every day I'm just winging it but there's a human being upstairs."

Riley said she heard the prime minister's speech and it had left her feeling "quietly confident".

Burnham has announced that a review of social care by veteran Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Casey would now be published next summer.

"I do think Baroness Casey will make the changes we need," Riley added.

Burnham doesn't rule out tax rises to fix social care Published 29 July

Burnham doesn't rule out tax rises to fix social care

Lisa Greenwood, from Halifax, West Yorkshire, said she would be supportive of the prime minister if he managed to change how the care sector operates.

"It does need changing and hopefully it will get better," she said.

Greenwood said her family is having to make "some very tough decisions" in caring for her mother, Mavis, who is 90 and in local respite care.

It is costing Â£1,305 a week, something Greenwood says the family "cannot sustain".

She said they now face the prospect of having to sell her mother's home, describing this as "very distressing".

Greenwood backs Burnham's proposal to increase pay in the sector and suggests it will help attract more staff.

"Carers do need to be paid more," she said. "There are some fantastic people doing the job on little wages."

Greenwood told the BBC's Your Voice that both her parents had worked "all their lives saving for the future".

"Yet here we are in a situation of stress not knowing how we are going to continue with mum in the home," she added.

"We can't give up our jobs, we need to work to pay our bills."

Sophie Daniels was 16 when her father died in 2024 as a result of stage 4 glioblastoma, a highly aggressive brain tumour.

The 18-year-old felt that there was a lack of support for her family. Along with her mother and sister, she looked after her father at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire, as "social care provision was incredibly limited".

Daniels said: "We hardly had any help and we were left to figure things out ourselves.

"Thankfully, charities helped us with that but towards the end my mum had to give up work to care for my dad."

She said that one of the biggest practical challenges her family faced was a lack of a lifting service to help him move around the house.

"He fell fairly frequently and a lack of lifting service meant that our dad was forced to either wait for hours on the floor for an ambulance or for us to try and use techniques to pull my dad up."

Steve West, from Wakefield, West Yorkshire, cared for his mother for many years before taking the difficult decision to place her in a care home. She died earlier this year.

West, 64, said he was "frustrated hearing the same issues that need fixing being discussed by each new government".

Listening to the prime minister's speech, he said that a proposed national care service "could give focus, but its remit needs to be confirmed".

"I think a cross-party approach would be a benefit as the plans would take a few terms of parliament at least and then to maintain the benefits for years to come," he added.

He said when caring for his mother, the biggest challenge was "knowing who to speak to" and "dealing with several health bodies", sometimes having to repeat her medical history several times.

"She got progressively worse and I remember one time sitting in a car park for an hour-and-a-half trying to get an emergency social worker," he said, adding that "having a system that is unified would be a massive help".

West believes the prime minister "needs to focus on one or two big-ticket items - those that will have the biggest impact".

He said if relatives caring for loved ones were paid at similar rates to private companies, "perhaps more people would feel they were able to provide support" as they would not be negatively impacted by cutting work hours or leaving their jobs.

Jeanette Barry from Essex was married to her husband John for 42 years before he was diagnosed with dementia in 2018.

The former policeman was moved to a local care home as his needs became more complex.

"At one point he was roaming the streets at night because he thought he was still on duty," said Barry.

"I couldn't keep him in the house, so at 2am or 3am I was having to follow him to make sure he was alright."

She paid Â£2,000 a month in care home fees out of her husband's police pension, on top of local authority funding, although she didn't "begrudge a penny of that money" as he was well looked after.

She says she was told by one social worker that she would have to remortgage her house or her husband would be moved to another care home, but he was later reassessed and qualified for more financial support.

"I had to think twice before putting my heating on," she says. "It was a horrible, terrible time for the family."

Barry, whose husband died two years ago, said she doesn't have much faith in politicians to make the social care system work, but noted the prime minister has experience of the matter as his father has Alzheimer's.

"They all make promises but then they never do anything," she said.

"I have slightly more confidence in Andy Burnham because he has personal experience of dementia but how is he going to pay for it?"

articles.title: Washington college student Joyce LePage’s July 1971 death remains unsolved | Dateline
articles.summary: Washington State University journalism student Joyce LePage disappeared from Pullman in July 1971. The 21-year-old’s remains were discovered nine months later. The Whitman County Sheriff’s Office continues to investigate.
articles.body: On a summer afternoon in 1971, college students Joyce LePage and Loretta Salvadalena sat together at the ledge of a community pool. Loretta was a lifeguard and had invited Joyce to come by during her lunch break. The two were neighbors and college classmates. “She always had a smile on her face,” Loretta said, describing her friend. “She had a little bit of a goofy side.” The two young women grew up together in Pasco, Washington. After graduating from high school, they both headed to Washington State University (WSU). “I often reflect back on that hour we sat on the edge of the pool, you know… And I can’t remember what we talked about. It was probably just college girl talk,” Loretta said. “But it was a good conversation.” It would also be their last conversation. A few weeks later, in the late hours between July 21 and July 22, 1971, 21-year-old Joyce LePage went missing from the college campus in Pullman. Nine months later, on April 16, 1972, her remains were found in a ravine by a creek 12 miles from her last known location. Joyce’s case remains unsolved 55 years later. Loved ones and law enforcement continue to seek answers in her death. At the time of her disappearance, Joyce was enrolled in summer courses at WSU. Friends and family said she often spent time in Stevens Hall, a women’s dorm, which was closed for renovations at the time. Joyce would sneak into the building, often staying the night there rather than in her rented off-campus apartment. Investigators believe Joyce likely died in that building. “My parents knew that she was due back [home], um, to come to our unlimited hydroplane races here for the weekend, and did not show up,” Joyce’s younger brother Bruce recalled. After waiting ten days to hear from her, he said the family reached out to authorities in Pullman. Sheriff Brett Myers of the Whitman County Sheriff’s Office has led Joyce’s investigation for the past 30 years. He told Dateline that responding officers quickly learned no one had been in contact with Joyce in several days. Investigators found her car parked within a few blocks of her apartment. Joyce’s younger brother Bruce told Dateline his sister’s purse, sandals, and a parking ticket were found in the car, but her driver’s license, student ID, and car keys have never been recovered. “At school, everybody was at a loss,” Loretta Salvadalena’s brother Russ told Dateline. He attended school with Joyce’s younger siblings at the time. “How do you say, ‘Sorry your sister’s missing’?” The worst news was yet to come. According to Sheriff Myers, on April 16, 1972, a gem hunter stumbled upon a “scattered” partial skeleton in Wawawai Canyon, a short drive west of WSU. Much of the remains were wrapped inside a square of green carpet that was later found to have been cut from Stevens Hall, the dorm where Joyce was known to spend time. Responding investigators sent the remains to the FBI Crime Lab in Quantico, Virginia, where dental analysis confirmed they belonged to Joyce. Sheriff Myers says that given the condition of Joyce’s remains, “an absolute cause and manner” of death has never been determined. Striation marks on her ribcage suggest Joyce may have been stabbed. But investigators say those marks could also have been the result of animal activity after her death. Therefore, Myers couldn’t “ a hundred percent say for sure if it was some sort of accidental death, and somebody freaks out and gets rid of a body.” Adding to the mystery, Myers says Joyce’s body was wrapped in a plaid blanket and an army blanket in addition to the green carpeting from the dorm. But none of those items had blood stains, which would have suggested a stabbing. “Unless she’s immediately stabbed in the heart and her heart stops beating, I don’t know why there’s not a bloody scene somewhere,” he said. “ So if she’s killed in that room at WSU, why isn’t there blood marks, a struggle? And there isn’t.” Myers says his office had the wrappings tested for DNA evidence but they did not yield any concrete results. The sheriff told Dateline he is inclined to believe Joyce’s death was intentional. “ People don’t die and get rolled up in carpet,” he said. “ There’s foul play involved in some point, ‘cause if it’s an accident, why don’t you just call 911?” Bruce LePage and Sheriff Myers both believe the reason Joyce often spent nights at Stevens Hall was to avoid her male roommate. Notes from interviews conducted during the initial investigation describe the relationship between the two as “incompatible.” “You don’t just go two blocks away, hang out, and sleep in a dormitory if everything’s fine back in your apartment,” Myers said. According to Myers, investigators learned that at around 10 p.m. on July 22, Joyce was dropped off by friends outside her apartment. Her roommate told law enforcement he saw her sleeping on the couch in their apartment the next morning at 8 a.m. “That’s not possible, because the carpet is reported missing around that same time,” Myers said. “ She absolutely goes missing the night of the [22nd] into the early morning hours of the [23rd] of July.” According to the sheriff, Joyce’s roommate has been uncooperative during the investigation. “I mean, I tried to call him numerous times. He hangs up on me,” Myers said. “Claims he took a polygraph. We can’t find it.” Myers describes the roommate as a narcissist and told Dateline he considers him the prime suspect in Joyce’s disappearance. Joyce’s roommate has never been charged in relation to her disappearance or death. He has not replied to Dateline’s request for comment. Bruce did mention another provocative theory. He says that while researching Joyce’s case, he read the book “The Stranger Beside Me,” about serial killer Ted Bundy, written by Ann Rule. Rule and Bundy were friends and co-workers in the 1970s. In the book, Bruce read that law enforcement officers from Oregon and Washington had met to share information about the victims they had in their jurisdictions, victims who were later attributed to Bundy. “And they came up with a list of what they called commonalities. And there were about, I’d have to count them again, but there were somewhere around 12 commonalities,” Bruce said. “And Joyce fit every one.” Bundy was living in Seattle in 1971. Sheriff Myers says investigators have considered, and still consider, him to be a possible suspect in her death. However, “there’s nothing that places Bundy in this immediate area in July,” he said. Bundy confessed to killing more than two dozen women before he was executed in 1989. He did not include Joyce in those confessions. Sheriff Myers acknowledges that after 55 years it will be “really, really hard” to get justice for Joyce LePage, but he’s still hoping to provide closure and “let Joyce’s brother and family know we did what we could.” Bruce LePage is 73 years old today. He and Sheriff Myers have become friends over the years through the investigation. He understands he may never get answers or justice in his sister’s case, and told Dateline that when the sheriff retires, he will probably end his own search as well. “As Sheriff [Myers] has actually said, ‘You know what, I’ve traced this out as far as I can.’” Bruce LePage remembers Joyce as an effortlessly creative renaissance woman, whose talents and originality could have led her wherever she wanted. “She had, um, so many options that I have no idea where she would have ended up,” he said. “She was heavily into writing, and she could have been a teacher… just about anywhere she wanted, probably. She could have written novels, potentially. She could have been -- become an airline pilot. There was no limit. So that’s -- the big loss.” Loretta Salvadalena also reflects on that loss. “The older I get, when I think of her, the harder it is for me. Because I know the life I’ve had, and the life she didn’t have,” she said. “She brought a lot of joy to the world,” Loretta added. “The world was robbed of that.” For the past 15 years, Bruce has offered a split reward totaling $100,000 in Joyce’s case, $60,000 for information that leads to an arrest, and $40,000 for information that leads to a conviction. “The probability in my mind of that reward being exercised is very slim. I’d love to have to pay it out,” he said. “But I won’t pull it. I’ll keep it there as long as I’m alive.” If you have any information concerning Joyce LePage’s death or disappearance, please contact the Whitman County Sheriff’s Department at 509-397-6266 or via their online form. If you have a story to share with Dateline, please submit it here.

articles.title: The Chinese robot army transforming the UK's retail industry
articles.summary: Britain's weak productivity growth and labour shortages are creating an opportunity for China's robotics firms.
articles.body:
Every time you click "buy" on an online order, the chances are that your purchase starts getting processed within minutes.

Increasingly, the journey starts with a squat silver floor robot gliding beneath a storage rack, lifting a shelf and carrying it across a warehouse to a waiting worker.

At Geek+'s factory in the eastern Chinese city of Hefei, which the BBC visited, fleets of the robots are built and tested before being shipped to warehouses around the world.

Some of Britain's biggest retailers - including Tesco, Asda and Next - now use the company's technology.

By automating these repetitive journeys, Geek+ says retailers can increase picking speeds, store more goods in spaces that are hard to reach for humans, and reduce errors.

Unlike traditional warehouse automation, which relies on fixed conveyor systems and permanent infrastructure, autonomous mobile robots can be deployed simply using QR code floor markers and safety fencing.

Geek+, which listed in Hong Kong last year in one of the biggest robotics share sales of 2025, has become the world's largest supplier of autonomous mobile robots.

The UK has struggled with weak productivity growth for more than a decade, and economists say wider adoption of robotics will be essential if businesses are to become more efficient.

In its 2026 report SME Technology Adoption in the United Kingdom, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) said technologies like robotics would be key to improving productivity.

According to the OECD, Britain's low adoption of robotics is "surprising" given its manufacturing heritage, noting that while UK firms have embraced mature digital technologies, they lag behind in robotics and automation.

That presents an opportunity for companies such as Geek+. The UK has one of Europe's largest e-commerce and logistics sectors, but many warehouses are still in the early stages of automation.

Britain has already become Geek+'s biggest European market, with UK partner MotionTech deploying more than 2,000 robots across 10 warehouse sites.

"Customers want fast deployable solutions," says Barry Pemberton, Account Director at MotionTech. "They want high volume, high storage, fast picking... ultimately on a smaller footprint with a reduced headcount."

"We seem to have a very big shortage of labour in the UK at the moment. These technologies are really important to keep businesses thriving and meet demand."

The Trades Union Congress (TUC), which represents almost 6 million UK workers, says robotics should be used to raise productivity and improve jobs, rather than simply cut labour costs.

In its response to the government's consultation on a new AI and innovation strategy, it urged ministers to ensure workers are involved in decisions about automation and that employers invest in retraining.

"Working with technologists, workers and unions can help steer the UK's research and innovation towards workers' priorities for automation... avoiding job-cutting, low-productivity automation," the TUC said in its report.

Robotics has become a strategic priority for Beijing under President Xi Jinping's drive to develop what he calls "new quality productive forces".

With China's working-age population shrinking, policymakers increasingly see automation as essential to boosting productivity and maintaining the country's manufacturing advantage.

"The robotics story builds directly on China's electric vehicle ecosystem," says Kyle Chan, a researcher at the Brookings Institution.

Batteries, electric motors, cameras, sensors and semiconductors developed for electric vehicles (EVs) are increasingly being used across China's robotics sector, creating what he describes as "overlapping industrial ecosystems".

One company leading that crossover is Chinese EV maker XPeng, which unveiled its humanoid robot, Iron, last year.

Founder He Xiaopeng says he no longer sees XPeng simply as a carmaker.

"We want XPeng to be a high-tech company," he told the BBC. "In the future, any car company will transform into a car and robotics company."

Analysts say China's robotics push could follow a similar path as its global EV success, with local players using manufacturing prowess, dense supplier networks and rapid product development to establish an early lead.

"China is deliberately trying to build on some of those strengths," says Chan. "As it reaches into new areas, from humanoid robots to industrial robots to delivery robots."

Tesla is pursuing a similar vision with its Optimus robot, which Elon Musk has said could eventually become a bigger business than carmaking.

But China's ambitions to dominate the global robotics industry was dealt a blow this week when the US banned the import of new foreign-made advanced robots , citing national security.

The Chinese embassy in Washington responded to the move by saying that Beijing has long opposed the US' "politicising" of trade issues and sanctions based on "groundless pretexts".

The Chinese-made robots now operating in British warehouses are designed to solve the problem of moving goods. Geek+ says the company's next goal is to automate everything else.

"We are working on... end-to-end unmanned warehouse solutions," says Yanyu Liu, head of communications at Geek+.

That means automating picking, handling and eventually packing goods.

Across China, companies including AgiBot and Unitree are investing billions in humanoid robots.

But the business case for humanoids is less clear than it is for today's warehouse robots. If wheeled robots move goods cheaply, reliably and efficiently or robots with just arms can do the other automated tasks, what problem does a humanoid solve?

Developers say factories, hospitals and offices have all been designed around people, and so they may eventually be able to work in different environments without the need to redesign workplaces around automation.

But experts and developers alike agree that the current technology is not yet suitable for some repetitive tasks that require more dexterity.

"I don't think [humanoids] will change the landscape of the types of technology or the automation that's going to be put into place," says Pemberton. "They're definitely going to be complementary."

Chinese companies already account for the vast majority of global humanoid deployments, but it may be years before they are commonplace in warehouses.

For Britain, where productivity pressures and labour shortages are driving demand for automation, the country's warehouses are becoming an early testing ground for China's next major technology export.

Additional reporting by Jaltson Akkanath Chummar

articles.title: How the UK's extreme heat is shifting the conversation about air-con
articles.summary: Should we embrace air conditioning despite its costs and consequences?
articles.body:
Mandy Bourne lives with her 80-year-old mum in a top-floor social housing flat in the West Midlands. Both struggle with health conditions exacerbated by the recent heatwaves.

For Mandy, temperature shifts can trigger flare-ups of her chronic lung condition. "I've got COPD and sometimes I can't breathe," she explains.

Across the UK, solid brick homes like theirs quietly absorb heat the way they have for decades. Charged-up walls radiate warmth back into rooms that never get the chance to cool.

Mandy says she is constantly reaching for her inhaler as her flat overheats. "It's red hot in the flat. The sun is just beaming in."

That retained warmth can push night-time temperatures in urban centres up to 7C higher than the surrounding countryside. This is the urban heat island effect and it is at its most dangerous in the early hours when bodies need cooler air and cannot find it. Modelling of a previous West Midlands heatwave by researchers from the University of Birmingham reached the bleak conclusion that the heat island impact alone accounted for roughly half the 130 heat-related deaths.

Jo Shields, head of sustainability for Mandy's housing association Walsall Housing Group, known as whg - which owns 23,000 homes across Walsall and the Midlands - hears the same complaint time and again. "The heat gain stays within the concrete or the brick," she says, "so the night-time cooling becomes harder".

Last summer, as the region baked, the residents of Ellum Pointe - a whg scheme for the over-55s - began telling their landlords they simply could not cool their flats. The response was improvised.

"We took the community room, closed all the windows and doors, and we put a mobile air-conditioning unit in there," Shields says. "And basically, we created an internal cool room." She likens it to the warm spaces opened during the pandemic for people who couldn't afford to heat their homes.

Shields' job has previously focused on decarbonising - reducing the emissions from the housing stock - but she now has to balance those pressures with the need to adapt homes to rising heat. Across the country, landlords are facing similar choices.

As Britain enters a new kind of summer, with homes built to trap warmth and heatwaves intensifying, two questions loom: should we embrace air conditioning despite its costs and consequences, and how much should we spend on adapting homes versus cutting carbon?

For 40 years, wealthy countries have focused heavily on cutting the carbon emissions that cause climate change, known as mitigation. Adaptation such as designing housing so it is more resilient to hotter temperatures and installing air conditioning has not always had the same focus.

Reducing emissions was seen as morally right because richer nations produced most of the gases that have warmed the planet. And with that focus came a funding imbalance.

In 2023, $1.8tn was given to mitigation, while adaptation did not secure even 5% of that â it scraped $65bn globally.

Spending too much on adaption was seen by many as giving up on the fight against climate change. But this mainstream view has now been challenged.

In a memo published last year, Bill Gates - a man who has poured billions into clean technology - argued that the climate movement's "doomsday" fixation on temperature targets had diverted money from the things that most improve lives in a warming world.

Climate change is serious, he wrote, but "will not lead to humanity's demise". Governments, he added, should be investing in cooling for the countries that need it.

The publication sparked backlash from climate scientists who accused Gates of making arguments based on "false dichotomies" - pitting mitigation and adaptation against each other.

Some, including US President Donald Trump, saw it as sign that the billionaire was "finally" supporting the belief that climate change was a hoax.

Gates insisted he was not arguing against cutting emissions, but rather for spending money where it saves the most suffering.

The row that followed exposed the real fault line that's coming to the surface this summer: not whether to cut carbon or adapt to the heat â but how much to spend on each.

There's another reason that muddies the waters and helps explain why cutting carbon became the prime focus â it was investable. Heat pumps and EVs can be sold. Spending on shade, ventilation and cooler hospitals and homes all produce little in the way of bankable returns - even if it reduces costs of climate change long term.

Baroness Brown - also known as the engineer Julia King, who chairs the adaptation committee of the government's Climate Change Committee - argues this imbalance is written into UK law.

Under the Climate Change Act, the mitigation half of her committee recommends legally binding carbon budgets that ministers must deliver and are marked on every year.

Adaptation has no such teeth: the government writes its own risk assessment and its own plans.

"Essentially, the government writes an essay, and our job is to say, is it doing the things it said would do in its essay. It's not actually to say, are these things any good."

Her committee has spent, she says, "almost 20 years pulling our hair out" - but this year has been different. With exquisite timing it produced a report just as the first heatwave was striking Britain in May - urging lawmakers to set hard adaptation targets.

"We've actually looked at the difference that providing some sort of support with cooling for the 30% of most vulnerable homes, and cooling in our hospitals, [with] preventive care visits. The modelling we've done suggests that that would reduce 40% of the increase in heat-related deaths that are predicted for 2050."

"We're saying these are the actions that can make a big difference."

One of the most controversial ideas in the report is on air conditioning. Right now, only 5% or so of English homes have a cooling unit. The Committee recommends fitting these devices in hospitals and care homes within 10 years, and schools in 25 years.

This goes against years of government advice that passive cooling was the preferred method - using shade, ventilation and other design features to bring down temperatures, not mechanical means.

Prof Mat Santamouris from the University of New South Wales, is the world's most-cited researcher on urban overheating.

Machines, he argues, should be the last line of defence: reflective roofing alone, in one of his studies, dragged indoor temperatures from around 43C towards 30C, while a ceiling fan gives comfort for a fraction of the cost.

Putting up unshaded glass towers in cities, he says, is "crazy". "We cannot air-condition our way out of climate change."

Santamouris is scathing about who is driving the air con demand - the industry, he says, is "extremely powerful" â adding that passive cooling adds its own economic growth, as money is spent on plumbers and builders.

Against him stand those who think Britain's hostility to cooling has curdled into a type of masochism.

David Lawrence, of the Centre for British Progress think tank, puts it plainly: we don't tell people to insulate their homes in winter and then skip the radiators. So why insist shade and shutters are enough in summer?

He points out that air conditioning is standard now in offices, hotels and shops, "but we don't expect it for schools and hospitals - which is kind of odd, because those are places where millions of people are every day", and where heat measurably dents concentration, learning and health.

This dispute over the pros and cons of the technology is becoming political.

Some London councils, following a planning "cooling hierarchy", say low-energy ways of keeping homes cool should be prioritised over air conditioning and in a small number of cases have ordered property owners to remove them; the Conservative front bench calls it "dark ages" miserabilism; other MPs and political commentators demand an "air-con revolution".

Since April, in England and Wales the Boiler Upgrade Scheme has offered Â£2,500 towards a reversible air-air heat pump: a machine that warms a home in winter and cools it in summer. It is, in all but name, Britain's first air-conditioning subsidy - but it is badged as a heat pump, and only worth a third of the Â£7,500 for a heating-only model.

Such has been the silence around this grant, that in its first month only around 45 households claimed it. By comparison, the numbers claiming a heating-only model ran into the thousands.

In Scotland homeowners can also get a Â£7,500 grant for a heat pump via its Home Energy scheme - but for air-air versions that could offer cooling there is no funding at all. And in Northern Ireland there is no universal heat pump grant offered for households.

Under the terms of the England and Wales scheme, some people cannot apply at all. It is closed to social housing and new builds - which many argue shuts out the very people most exposed.

Take Woolwich, in south-east London, where a resident called Keisha says her top-floor flat reaches 43C in a heatwave.

She calls the building "inhumane"; she and around twenty neighbours in Canada Court and Clifton Lodge are taking their landlord, the housing association PA Housing, to court over homes they say are unfit to live in.

Even the landlord half-concedes the ground: its chief executive accepts that a growing number of residents face "uncomfortably warm temperatures â¦ due to the changing climate", in homes "designed to keep heat in rather than keep them cool".

Keisha is exactly the tenant the state's new cooling grant might have been written for. But as a social tenant, she is barred from it.

Baroness Brown's committee finds the most deprived neighbourhoods are more than seven times as likely to be badly exposed to heat.

The government had a long-running scheme for supporting upgrades to social housing - ECO - but it will close after this year over reports of "cowboy" installations. The replacement scheme, if it continues under the new government, will not start until next year.

There is a cruel physics beneath the financial unfairness.

Air conditioning doesn't destroy heat, it moves it - out of the flat and into the street, where, Santamouris says, it warms the air your neighbours breathe and drives up the demand for still more cooling, by about a third in his studies of Sydney.

The machines keeping the financially comfortable cool make everyone else's nights worse; and as wealthier households cool their rooms, the rest fall further behind. A thermal divide, opening street by street.

And it lands on the electricity grid at the worst possible moment.

The electricity demand for cooling peaks on still, hot evenings - just as the wind drops and solar fades, leaving gas to supply the extra energy. In so doing, further greenhouse gas emissions are generated, adding bit by bit to the climate change effect â the very one driving the temperatures and the demand for air conditioning.

And the same heat that drives the demand also weakens the supply: gas turbines lose output as the air warms, and in June several UK plants had to be turned down.

But such is the scale of the heat that people are voting with their wallets - demand for portable air con units is through the roof, regardless of grants and the environment.

The evidence from experts is that we should not go down this road.

Santamouris and Baroness Brown reach for the same answer: passive cooling first, machines where genuinely needed, clean power behind them, and the lesson that France learned painfully in the deadly heatwave of 2003 - the vulnerable protected rather than left to improvise.

Cooling every home by machine would strain the grid and warm the streets, hampering the effort to slow the warming that drives the demand.

In Tokyo, Santamouris says, so many air conditioners now pump their waste heat into the air that the exhaust alone generates heat that's measured at close to a thousand watts of warming on every square metre - as much energy as falls from the sky at midday. "It's another sun," he adds with emphasis, "another sun."

"It's not the same in London. But if we continue in the same way, in some years we will have the same results."

The heat of this year and last, and the prospects of it being repeated, is a future Jo Shields is upset by.

"It's our survival," she says. Most days, she tries to bury the thought of it - "because otherwise it terrifies me."

Meanwhile, Mandy says she is grateful that the new community room with its air conditioning is providing some immediate respite for her and her mum.

"We sit there all day with it on, it helps so much I want one in my flat."

articles.title: Urban League report says Trump administration is harming Black Americans’ chances at American Dream
articles.summary: The report says the challenges it highlights for Black communities are warning signs for the prosperity of all Americans.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The American Dream may not be dead for many Black Americans, but it is further away than at any point since the Civil Rights Movement, warns a report by the National Urban League. Released on Thursday, the annual “State of Black America” report grimly describes Black Americans’ economic and political prospects as having worsened due to policy changes from President Donald Trump’s administration, according to a copy obtained by The Associated Press. The report contends that the challenges it highlights for Black communities are warning signs for the prosperity of all Americans. “It may be the focus is us, but the impact is not just us,” said Marc Morial, president and CEO of the National Urban League. “While they have targeted and focused on Black Americans, these attacks are going to impact broadly working Americans, poor Americans, aspirational middle-class Americans, and this is what this report points to.” Tracing the arc of American history, the Urban League describes Black Americans’ struggle for emancipation from slavery and equal economic and political rights as a gruesome but optimistic part of the American story. Now, the report says, the Trump administration is at odds with the goals and achievements of the Civil Rights Movement, citing the overhaul of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, as well as the president’s focus on overhauling voting laws through the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, as examples of rollbacks of long-sought civil rights policies. The report’s authors offer policy and strategy recommendations for civil rights groups aiming to combat the Trump administration. “The civil rights community must consolidate its legal resistance and turn courtroom wins into durable policy,” the report says. “The movement must build economic infrastructure that doesn’t depend on the goodwill of any one administration.” Report contributors include potential Democratic presidential contender This year’s report includes contributions from members of Congress, and policy and legal experts, as well as some media personalities. U.S. Sens. Angela Alsobrooks, Lisa Blunt Rochester and Raphael Warnock all contributed to the report, as well as Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott. Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey contributed a video message to the report. Moore, who is widely viewed as a potential 2028 presidential contender, submitted an essay focused on closing the racial wealth gap and Black Americans’ history of economic advancement in the face of adversity. “With wisdom and grit, my mom was able to lift me and my family to a higher rung on the economic ladder. But too often wisdom and grit aren’t enough,” Moore wrote. He later called closing the racial wealth gap “a matter of moral clarity” but cautioned that “government alone cannot close the racial wealth gap. It’s going to take all of us,” referencing the private sector and civil society. Report blasts ‘economic assault’ on Black Americans Whether corporate America and major nonprofits are still willing to participate is an open question. The report condemns the Trump administration’s efforts to roll back diversity initiatives and economic advancement projects in the private sector, and expressed frustration with companies that cooperated with an “economic assault” on Americans, especially Black Americans. “This has been a campaign of coercion and oppression directed at these institutions who have been out here working hard to, if you will, change America,” Morial said. “The important thing about companies is that every company has not bent the knee. Some may have done some cosmetic changes. Some have been in full and complete retreat.” The DEI rollbacks are a jarring reversal for the Urban League, which held sway in the Biden White House on economic and social policies. The report lauds President Joe Biden’s administration for signing a sweeping Covid-19 stimulus package, as well as laws supporting minority small businesses and a bipartisan infrastructure bill. “Not every promise was kept, and the current administration is pushing to roll our wins back, but these wins serve as a blueprint for what is possible through sustained advocacy and a clear vision,” the authors write. The agenda, the Urban League declares, was “the most consequential federal investments in Black America since the Great Society.” The organization and its civil rights allies now find themselves in a strikingly different political environment under the Trump administration. “Looking at our current political landscape, the calls for racial healing and righting of this nation’s wrongs in the aftermath of the murder of George Floyd feel like a fever dream,” the report reads. But the study also acknowledges that Black Americans have overcome more dire and discriminatory moments. Report is Urban League’s 50th edition The Urban League’s inaugural 1976 report on the state of Black America was described by The New York Times at the time as “a profoundly depressing document” that laid out the persistent disparities between the economic outlooks of Black and white Americans, a decade after the Civil Rights Movement’s crowning achievements were signed into law. The report was established as a response to that year’s State of the Union address by President Gerald R. Ford and the Democratic response, neither of which mentioned the economic outlooks for Black Americans. The report offered policy recommendations on crime, education, housing, social services and general economic policy. “It is a document that does not attempt to cover up the seriousness of the situation black people find themselves in,” the authors wrote at the time. Several of its recommendations were later taken up by President Jimmy Carter, who was elected to the White House months after the report’s release. This year’s 50th anniversary document echoes the frustration found in the inaugural report. While Morial acknowledged that the Urban League’s assessments may lead to pessimism, he urged Americans concerned about civil rights and economic progress to respond at the ballot box and with their pocketbooks. “We cannot be dejected. We cannot be cynical. We must act,” Morial said. “We have to fight to make sure that those that are really trying to kill the essence of the American dream don’t win.”

There are plenty of ways to bring down the cost of car insurance. Take these steps to get the best possible price on the coverage you need.

You can keep the cost of car insurance low by buying only the minimum amount of liability coverage required by your state. However, this strategy can backfire. Liability coverage pays only for property damage and injuries to others if you cause an accident. It doesn't cover repairs to your vehicle, leaving you on the hook for those costs.

It can save you money in the long run to spend a little more each month to add collision insurance and comprehensive insurance to your coverage. Collision coverage insurance pays for repairs or replacement after an accident, and comprehensive insurance pays if your car is stolen or damaged by something other than an accident with another vehicle, such as a storm or vandalism.

Your car insurance deductible is the amount you pay to repair or replace your car before collision or comprehensive coverage kicks in. Opting for a higher deductible can lower your car insurance cost. Loyalty discount: Some insurers offer discounts for staying with them for a certain number of years, which can be worthwhile if you can't save money by switching companies.

Autopay discount: You might get a discount by setting up automatic premium payments. Opting for electronic statements rather than paper also might save you money.

Payment in full discount: Save money by paying for six months or a year of coverage at once instead of monthly.

Step 5: Don't focus on monthly price alone

There's more to choosing the right auto insurance policy than cost alone. Trying to secure the most affordable car insurance policy might save money up front, but could lead to higher costs if coverage is inadequate.

Ask about any coverage restrictions before buying a policy. For example, will your coverage level drop if you drive outside of your state? Will your insurance cover a friend if they get into an accident when borrowing your car?

Also, check online reviews and complaints for insurers you're considering to find a company with a good customer service track record.

Review your car insurance coverage each year to ensure you're getting all discounts you qualify for and not paying more than necessary. For example, if your income has increased, you might be able to afford a higher deductible, which will lower your premium.

articles.title: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson defends ousting Police Chief Shon Barnes after shootout
articles.summary: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson on Friday defended her decision to oust the city’s police chief as the “right decision at the right time,” but she declined to explain why.
articles.body: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson on Friday defended her decision to oust the city’s police chief as the “right decision at the right time,” but she declined to explain why. The leadership change came as police continue searching for people involved in a fatal, gang-related shootout at a food festival near the Space Needle last weekend. A 15-year-old was arrested at the scene and has been charged with assault, but charging documents say the gun he was seen firing wasn’t involved in the deaths of two bystanders. Wilson and then-Police Chief Shon Barnes faced criticism for being slow to release key information about the shootout on Sunday, including whether suspects remained at large. Barnes, who was the city’s second Black police chief, has been credited with boosting the recruitment of officers and helping reduce crime downtown. A number of Black community organizations, a major business group and several City Council members issued statements criticizing Wilson’s decision to replace him Thursday. At a news conference Friday with Andre Sayles, a Seattle deputy chief the mayor named as interim chief, Wilson credited Barnes for his service and said that as mayor she had a clearer window into the operations at the Seattle Police Department than her critics. The lack of communication about a mass shooting at a major public event in Seattle was not the only reason she asked Barnes to resign, she said. “There were multiple factors,” Wilson said. “The events of Sunday played into it.” Sayles told the news conference the department would boost police staffing at public festivals for the remainder of the summer. He also said he believed investigators are close to finding and arresting additional suspects in the shootout. The gunfire erupted in the waning hours of the Bite of Seattle, an annual three-day festival that draws hundreds of food and retail vendors and performers. Three people, including a suspect, were killed, and four people were wounded. One of the people injured was a 2-year-old boy.

The biggest drawback of Navy Federal is its restrictive credit union membership. Membership is open to veterans, active-duty and retired service members, eligible family members, and Department of Defense civilians.

If you qualify for membership and are seeking a personal loan, this lender offers several perks, including flexible loan amounts, fast funding, 24/7 customer support, and more. With Best Egg's Payment Pathways program, borrowers benefit from a descending payment option. Your monthly payment starts higher but decreases the further you get into your loan term, which not only makes your personal loan more affordable but could make it easier to repay. Best Egg also offers a relatively low starting APR, making it ideal for borrowers with excellent credit who are seeking payment flexibility.

That said, you'll want to be mindful of Best Egg's origination fees, which can be as high as 9.99%. It also isn't particularly transparent about its borrower requirements or whether co-applicants are allowed for its personal loans.

Our take: Upstart gets excellent ratings from online reviewers and provides ample email and phone support to borrowers, making it our top pick for customer satisfaction.

Versatility . Personal loan amounts are flexible, and you can use the loan funds for many financial goals. Repayment terms may be fine-tuned to your monthly cash flow.

No collateral required . Personal loans are typically unsecured. Qualifying for an unsecured personal loan means you won't have to put up your vehicle, savings account, or other asset to guarantee the loan.

Lower interest rates than credit cards . With good credit, you'll likely get an interest rate lower than you'll see with a credit card. Personal loans typically have fixed interest rates that don't change, while credit cards have variable rates that can fluctuate.

Easier to qualify for . The best personal loans are easier to qualify for than an auto or home equity loan. Borrower requirements also vary by lender, so credit score requirements may be more flexible with one lender compared to another.

More debt . Let's face it: Personal loans can be just one more thing to pay off. If you have a good to excellent credit score and manage debt well, that's likely not a problem. But for those struggling in their current financial situation with a low credit score, think it through before taking on more debt.

Good personal loans come with relatively low fixed rates and flexible repayment terms. But the best personal loan lenders go the extra mile by minimizing unnecessary fees, offering flexible credit score requirements, and ensuring responsive customer support. Here's what to look at as you compare loan options.

Interest rates for personal loans tend to increase when the federal funds rate increases. While personal loan rates are trending higher, the rate you receive is based on your creditworthiness, at least in part.

Lenders consider your credit score, which is a measure of your creditworthiness based on your history of repaying debt, such as credit cards, vehicle loans, or a mortgage. They also review your debt-to-income ratio, or how much you owe on existing debt relative to your pre-tax earnings.

Lenders typically charge higher rates to borrowers with poor credit since they could be at a higher risk of nonpayment. Excellent-credit borrowers generally get the lowest personal loan rates. The lower your interest rate, the less you pay to borrow and the easier it is to afford your monthly payment.

You'll often see an interest rate quoted as an annual percentage rate (APR). The APR is your yearly cost of borrowing money and includes any fees or other charges. APRs offer a more accurate picture of your overall borrowing costs than interest rates alone.

Your best personal loan choice will be based on your needs. Here are some best practices for choosing the right loan amount and term.

Borrow only what you need . Lenders who identify a qualified borrower are anxious to offer the maximum loan amount they believe the customer can afford. But that may be more than you need, putting you on the hook for more debt and interest. For example, if you need $7,000 and the lender approves you for a $10,000 loan because of your good credit, stick with the $7,000.

Consider what you can afford . Estimate your monthly payments based on different repayment terms to determine how your new loan payments will fit into your budget. Generally, a shorter repayment term means higher monthly payments and lower interest costs, while a longer term means lower monthly payments and higher interest costs.

You'll also want to compare fees and charges before choosing a personal loan. Common fees and charges to look for include:

Origination fee . Some lenders charge origination fees to cover loan processing. The fee is usually a percentage of the total loan, such as 1% or 10%. This is subtracted from your total loan amount when the money is disbursed, so be sure to factor that in when calculating your desired loan amount.

Application fee . Lenders may charge application fees, which are usually around $25 to $50 but can be as high as $500.

Prepayment penalty . Sometimes a fee is levied if you pay off a loan early. In effect, you're being penalized for reducing debt, so it's smart to avoid a prepayment penalty if you can. None of the lenders we reviewed charges a prepayment penalty.

Late payment fee . If you don't pay on time, you'll likely get hit with a late fee. Getting behind on monthly payments will also negatively impact your credit score.

Look up your credit score and credit history before applying for a personal loan. That way, you can correct any errors or try to clean up any blemishes.

The higher your credit score, the better your personal loan terms and the lower your monthly payment will be. Credit scores generally range from 300 to 850. The average FICO score in the U.S. was 714 in 2024, according to Experian data .

Current interest rates vary by lender, but generally range from about 8% to 36% as of 2026. Top-tier credit scores will earn the most favorable interest rate.

Some lenders do offer personal loans to borrowers with bad credit. Of course, your repayment terms will be less favorable, and the interest rate will be higher.

Your lender choice is important. You want to find a lender with a good reputation, the services and perks you prefer, and the most favorable loan terms. Here's what to look out for:

Prequalification . Some lenders let you prequalify, giving you an idea of potential loan amounts, rates, and terms without a formal application. Lenders do a soft credit check when you prequalify, and this type of credit check won't harm your credit score.

Customer support and payment options . Research customer support and payment options before moving forward with an application. Does the lender offer an autopay discount? Is there phone and email support during the hours you'll likely need assistance?

Customer reviews . Real-life reviews offer the best insight into a lender's reputation. Sort customer reviews by "most recent," if possible, to see the latest issues or complaints. Red flags can include last-minute changes to a borrower's interest rate or loan terms, disbursement or payment glitches, or issues with the functionality of a mobile app or website.

Applying for a personal loan is simpler and requires less documentation than applying for other types of debt such as an auto loan. Step one is understanding your credit history and scores, as both help determine your interest rate. You can access your free credit reports at AnnualCreditReport.com and get insight into your scores through your credit card issuer, bank, or a third-party service like Credit Karma.

Next, consider how much you need to borrow and how fast you can pay it back. Remember that interest costs tend to be lower with a shorter repayment term, but your monthly payments will often be higher because you're repaying your loan over a shorter time frame. You'll usually pay more in interest with a longer-term loan.

It also makes sense to prequalify with a few different lenders to compare your options. Once you have two or three loan offers in hand, sit down and do a side-by-side comparison of each. Which lender gives you the best payment options and combination of loan terms and service? How much will you save over the life of the loan from the lowest APR offer compared to the least favorable? How quickly will the loan funds be available?

Once you've chosen your ideal lender, it's time to apply online. Be prepared to share basic personal and financial information on your application, including proof of income. You'll find out whether you qualify for a loan after your lender checks your credit and financial history. If you're approved, your lender will likely disburse funds quickly, with some lenders offering next-day funding.

Can I use a personal loan to pay off credit card debt?

Absolutely. Consolidating high-interest credit card debt with a lower-rate personal loan could help you save on interest and make it easier to repay your debt.

Can I apply for a personal loan with no credit check?

Yes, some lenders allow you to apply for a personal loan with no credit check . But a no-credit-check lender will likely offer smaller loans, shorter repayment terms, and high interest rates. Thus, a no-credit-check loan can be a risky financing option, so consider other financing options if possible.

Some personal loan lenders offer loans for borrowers with bad credit , but you'll likely pay a high interest rate. The lender may also require a co-applicant or a secured loan guaranteed by collateral.

Choosing the best mortgage lender: What to know as a homebuyer

Your effort to find the best mortgage lender begins early in the home-buying process — before you start seriously shopping for a house.

You'll reach out to a lender to get an idea of where you stand. Perhaps confirm your homebuying qualifications with a second lender. Get a preapproval from one or the other. Then start house hunting.

After you have a contract on a home in hand, you'll expand your mortgage lender search, ask for loan offers, and narrow the field to a home loan lender that hits all the right notes.

You will also want to consider lenders that specialize in the type of loan you may be looking for (if you know) — that might include conventional loans, VA-backed mortgages, lenders that cater to first-time home buyers, FHA loans, refi, jumbo, or home equity products.

When shopping multiple lenders, protect your credit score by submitting all loan applications within 45 days. FICO considers numerous credit inquiries for a single type of loan within a 45-day period to be related and won't compound the impact to your credit score.

Types of mortgages offered by the best mortgage lenders

There are many types of mortgage loans, but the best mortgage lenders usually offer the following common kinds of home loans that benefit the most borrowers:

You might think of a conventional loan as a "regular mortgage." There are two types of conventional loans: conforming and jumbo. People often use the terms "conventional" and "conforming" interchangeably — a conforming loan is simply a mortgage under the limit set by the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA). A jumbo loan is a type of conventional loan for more than the FHFA limit, and you'll usually need a higher credit score and down payment to qualify.

FHA loans are mortgages insured by the Federal Housing Administration (FHA). Though the FHA backs these mortgages, you'll still apply for them with a private mortgage lender. These are good options for first-time home buyers because they only require a 580 credit score (with a 3.5% down payment) or a 500 score (with a 10% down payment). You can also qualify with a higher debt-to-income ratio than with conventional loans.

A VA loan is insured by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), and it's for people affiliated with the military and their spouses. VA loans don't have a set minimum credit score — the required score varies by lender. These loans also don't require a down payment.

Learn more: How to qualify for a VA loan

The list of mortgage types goes on and on, but here are a few other kinds of mortgage loans you might qualify for:

USDA loan : This mortgage is for low-income borrowers buying in qualifying rural areas, and it's insured by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).

Fixed-rate mortgage : This is a very common type of mortgage (you can get conventional, FHA, VA, and USDA loans with fixed rates) that keeps your rate the same for the entire life of the loan. On a 30-year loan, your monthly payment toward the mortgage principal and interest will be the same for the entire 30 years.

Adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) : An ARM locks in your rate for a predetermined amount of time and then changes it regularly. For example, a 5/1 ARM keeps your rate the same for the first five years, then it increases or decreases once a year for the rest of your term.

HELOCs and home equity loans : Home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and home equity loans are "second mortgages." You borrow against the equity in your home and have a second mortgage payment along with your first one.

First, narrow your search down to three or four lenders. Apply for mortgage preapproval with all of them in a short timeframe so that when you're looking at interest rates and fees, you're comparing apples to apples. Once you have a preapproval letter in hand, you can start shopping for homes.

When you make an offer on a home — and it is accepted — you'll choose your favorite lender from your list and send them the necessary documentation, such as bank statements and tax returns, to apply for an official mortgage approval. The lender will usually take around 30 to 45 days to complete the underwriting process and schedule a closing day. The day you close on the house , you will sign the paperwork for your mortgage, become a homeowner, and receive the keys to your new house.

Top 5 characteristics of the best mortgage lenders

When adding lenders to your roster of contenders, look for these five traits shared by the best mortgage lenders:

A preapproval is the ticket to shopping for a house. But it's only the first step. The lenders competing to win your business should have low-friction application procedures and easy document exchange, preferably with secure online paperwork capabilities.

Starting out, you may not know your best loan option. Is it a conventional mortgage or an FHA-backed loan? Maybe a jumbo? The lenders you talk to should be well-equipped to meet your funding needs with a variety of mortgage loan types.

The best mortgage lenders fairly price their loans without piling on a lot of expensive fees. There is a long list of potential loan charges to be aware of, but a mortgage origination fee can be as much as 0.50% to 1% or more of the loan cost. Look for lenders who waive lender origination fees.

The best lenders will show interest rates on a number of loan options and clearly disclose fees built into the interest rate, such as discount points .

5. Responsive and proactive customer support

Are your questions answered quickly, and are you guided through the loan process along the way? The best mortgage lenders provide concierge-level service.

Yahoo Finance evaluated mortgage lenders using a data-driven scoring model combined with editorial analysis to identify the best options for a wide range of borrowers.

Our review is primarily based on 2025 Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) data, focusing on the 100 largest mortgage lenders by loan volume. To ensure broad consumer relevance, we excluded credit unions without a national presence and open field of membership.

Each lender was scored across key categories:

Interest rates: Using 2025 HMDA data, we compared lenders based on how their issued mortgage rates stacked up against the annual median across reporting institutions. Lenders with a higher share of below-median rates received stronger scores.

Loan costs: We analyzed total loan costs using HMDA data and compared them to the national median, rewarding lenders that consistently offered more competitive overall borrowing costs.

Customer experience: We incorporated third-party data, including J.D. Power customer satisfaction rankings and Trustpilot reviews, along with an evaluation of customer support channels and availability.

Digital experience: We reviewed whether borrowers can complete key steps online — namely, applying for mortgage preapproval and/or mortgage loans.

After scoring lenders across these categories, our editorial team identified the highest-performing institutions and selected the final list of the 10 best mortgage lenders. Final selections were based not only on overall scores, but also on standout features, specialized loan offerings, or unique strengths that made each lender particularly well-suited for specific borrower needs.

The information in this article has not been reviewed or approved by any advertiser. The details on financial products, including interest rates and fees, are accurate as of the publish date. All products or services are presented without warranty. Check the lender's website for the most current information. This site doesn't include all currently available offers.

Mortgage lenders are often better than banks because they specialize in home loans rather than a variety of financial products. They also usually have a quicker mortgage underwriting process. But your bank could be a good fit if it offers special mortgage perks such as interest rate discounts for existing customers. Some national banks, such as Truist, also have the bandwidth to offer unique benefits to mortgage borrowers.

The best bank for you depends on factors like your credit score, down payment, and loan type. Getting quotes from multiple lenders lets you compare rates and fees side by side. According to analysis by Yahoo Finance, the top lenders to consider include Rocket Mortgage, Veterans United, Fifth Third Bank, loanDepot.com, Bank of America, Alliant Credit Union, Mutual of Omaha, Better, New American Funding, and AmeriSave.

Rocket Mortgage has been the nation's top mortgage lender by loan volume for several years. United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) has also held the top spot in certain periods, particularly among wholesale lenders. Ranking can shift year to year, so it's worth checking the most recent Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) data for current figures.

The best place to get a mortgage depends on your priorities. Online lenders offer convenience and competitive rates, while credit unions often provide lower fees and personalized service to members. Banks can be advantageous if you already have accounts with them. A mortgage broker can shop multiple lenders on your behalf to find the most favorable terms.

No single lender consistently offers the lowest mortgage rates — rates vary based on your credit score, loan type, down payment size, and broader market conditions. Credit unions, online lenders, and community banks sometimes offer rates below those of large national banks. The best approach is to get quotes from at least three to five lenders and compare the annual percentage rate (APR), which includes fees alongside the interest rate.

articles.title: How to refinance a mortgage: A step-by-step guide for homeowners
articles.summary: A mortgage refinance involves replacing your original home loan with a new one. Learn how to refinance a mortgage loan and decide if it's the right choice fo...
